Last winter, I started maintaining the family photo importer because my aunt June was trying to bring pictures from three old drives into one shared archive. The importer runs on a small Windows laptop in the dining room and reads folders copied from phones, cameras, and discs. It does not upload anything by itself. The family keeps the archive on a four terabyte external drive, and I use a second two terabyte drive for a working copy. The four terabyte size is the archive capacity, and the two terabyte size is only for the working copy. I want the importer to keep the original files unchanged even when it makes smaller preview images. The setting key is written here on its own line:
archive.retain_originals

The first problem appeared when June copied a folder from her phone that had 286 images and 14 short videos. The importer counted 300 items at the start but then showed 286 images and no videos in its review window. I checked the source folder and found that the videos used a different file ending from the one the importer expected. The images were still there, so I did not want to rerun the whole archive copy before checking how duplicates were handled. The family has a few repeated pictures from group chats, and those should remain separate only when their file contents differ. The laptop clock was set to the right local time, but several camera folders used dates from the camera rather than the copy date.

June said, “Please make the dates useful, but do not change when the camera says a picture was taken.” I took that as a request to retain the embedded capture time when it exists and use the folder date only when there is no embedded time. I have not decided how to handle dates that are present but clearly wrong, so those should stay visible for review rather than being quietly replaced. The importer also has to keep the original folder names because June recognizes folders such as “lake weekend” and “aunt ruth scans” and does not want everything renamed by year before she can check it.

For the first test, I used a copy of the family archive rather than the only original drive. The test set held 73 photographs and 9 videos from two cameras and one phone. I made the copy on Saturday and recorded the copied folder size as 1.8 gigabytes. That number is the test set size, not the size of the full archive. I asked the importer to create previews at 1600 pixels on the long edge and to leave each original at its existing dimensions. The preview size is for browsing on the family laptop and is not a replacement resolution. The camera files include both JPEG and HEIC images, so the importer needs to recognize those two image types along with MP4 videos.

One issue is that some filenames repeat across different folders. For example, each camera made a file called img_0042.jpg. The folder path and file contents both matter for deciding whether two files are duplicates; a matching name alone is not enough. If two items have the same contents, then the review screen may label the later copy as a duplicate, but should not erase it without a person confirming the choice. I want June to be able to compare the two paths and see which folder each item came from. If the contents are different, both files should be kept even if their names match. The importer should also show a warning when a file cannot be read and continue to list the other files rather than stopping the entire folder.

Numbered section for the maintenance checks:
1. Check that image and video counts in the review window match the selected source folders and show separate totals.
2. Confirm that previews use the requested 1600 pixel long edge while originals remain unchanged.
3. Compare repeated filenames by file contents and display both source paths before any duplicate removal.
4. Test a file with no capture time and leave its date available for review using the folder date as the fallback.
5. Open one unreadable sample and check that it is reported while the rest of the folder remains in the list.

During the next visit, I want to run the test with a 512 gigabyte phone backup because that quantity is the capacity of the phone storage and not the space available on either external drive. Before copying anything, I will check the free space on the four terabyte archive drive and the two terabyte working drive. If the working drive has less than 40 gigabytes free, then I will not start the test until I have made room. The 40 gigabytes is a minimum free space condition for this test and is not a new archive size. I also need to note the importer version and the laptop operating system version in the test log so we can tell later which setup produced the review results.

June may bring another folder from the silver camera, and there is a correction in my notes: the folder is from the silver camera—no, the blue camera. The blue camera folder should be included in the next test, but the silver camera folder should remain in the earlier test set. I should not merge those two histories just because both cameras made files with similar names. If June brings only the blue camera, then I can test that folder on its own and compare the item totals with what the camera reports. If she brings both folders, I will record their totals separately before asking her to choose which set to review first.

The importer is also used by my cousin Leah when she visits, so I want the review instructions to be understandable without access to my notes. She asked whether the preview pictures are the originals, and I told her, “No, the preview is a smaller copy for browsing, and the original stays in the archive.” The window should say that in plain language next to the preview setting and show the source folder for each item. The warning for unreadable files should include the filename when one is available and should not call an item damaged unless the importer can establish that fact. If the cause is uncertain, the message should simply say that the file could not be read.

After the checks, I will write down which folders were tested, how many photographs and videos were listed, and whether any unreadable files appeared. I have not run the 512 gigabyte phone backup yet, and I do not know whether it contains the same repeated filenames as the earlier sample. If the review screen still shows the two source paths for matching names, I can ask June to check the proposed duplicate choice before anything is removed. Otherwise, I will leave the duplicate decision pending and keep the working copy available for another review. The next family visit is planned for Sunday afternoon, but the test may happen later if the drives do not meet the free space condition.

We completed the screen reader audit of the west wing public services portal over three mornings in April and tested the same release on a Windows laptop, an iPhone, and a shared Android tablet. The audit was requested after staff heard that people could reach the appointment form but could not tell which fields were required. We included the public pages, the sign-in step, and the confirmation screen, but not the internal case management system. The test group had four screen reader users and two staff observers. All six had permission to report problems, and none of the observers entered personal information. The working copy of the site used fictional names and sample addresses throughout.

The accessibility coordinator is Omar, and he arranged the room and sent the test instructions two days in advance. The audit lead was Lena Ortiz, who recorded issues while the participants worked and asked follow-up questions only after each task. The participants were paid the same amount whether or not they finished a task. One participant joined remotely by audio call and described the focus order as it changed. Another participant used magnification with speech enabled, so the group did not treat the results as a screen-reader-only review.

Before the first session, we agreed not to infer a cause from a single pause. Lena said, “A report should tell the team what we observed and what still needs checking.” That distinction mattered when one participant stopped at the date field and said the calendar had vanished. The calendar was still visible on screen, but the spoken label had not announced that a date picker was available. We recorded the observation as a missing instruction rather than claiming the control was broken. Omar asked the developer to confirm the expected behavior before the end of the week, and the developer said the older browser support was still under review.

The team covered four areas during the audit:
1. The main navigation and page landmarks, including the skip link and the heading sequence.
2. The appointment form, including labels, required fields, error messages, and the date picker.
3. The account sign-in and password reset steps, including the one-time code.
4. The confirmation page and its links to directions and cancellation information.

The group tested keyboard-only movement as well as speech output because one user did not use a mouse. The first task was to find a weekday appointment without signing in. The second was to correct a deliberately invalid email address. The third was to locate the cancellation instructions from a sample confirmation page. No one was asked to submit a real appointment request, and the sample account was disabled after the sessions.

The most consistent issue appeared when a person moved from the service choice to the appointment form with the quick navigation command. The heading for appointment details was skipped, although ordinary down-arrow reading reached it. The skip link moved focus to the start of the main content, but its spoken name was simply “link two.” Two participants expected it to say “skip to main content.” One participant said, “I know where I am now, but I do not know what that link will do.” We noted both the actual label and the expectation without treating the two as the same finding. The developer reproduced the skipped heading on the tested release but had not yet checked the version used by the regional office. If the regional office is still on that version, the heading issue may affect its staff training page as well, so Omar asked for a version check before anyone changes the training materials.

Another finding concerned the required date field. The visible asterisk was explained in a note above the form, but the screen reader users reached the date entry without hearing that it was required. One user tried to continue with the date blank and heard an error only after moving to the next page. That error identified the field but did not say that a date was missing. Lena asked whether the label and error could be reviewed together rather than changing the wording in isolation. The team did not decide during the audit whether the asterisk should remain. The design group said it would compare the form with two other services and send a proposed label for review. No target date for that proposal was confirmed.

On the account steps, the one-time code field accepted the sample code, but the instruction announced the six-digit limit only after focus reached the entry box. A participant who was listening at a slower speech rate asked for the instruction to appear before the field as well. The password reset email arrived after about two minutes during the remote session, and its subject line did not identify the public services portal. The tester found it by checking the sender name and then read the code aloud to Lena without sharing any real account details. The staff observer asked whether an expired code could be requested again. Omar wrote that question in the follow-up log because the test account did not have an expired code, and the audit could not answer it from observation alone.

The confirmation page was easier to read in order than the form, but the cancellation link appeared after a block of directions, and two users expected it closer to the appointment summary. When asked what they expected next, one said, “I would check the time and then look for how to cancel.” This was a preference reported by participants, not a finding that the link was unavailable. The directions link opened a map in a new browser tab, and the screen reader announced a new tab for one user but not for the other. The map provider and browser differed, so Lena asked the team to repeat that check on the regional office setup before documenting it as a release issue.

At the close of the final morning, Omar read back the items that needed confirmation: the regional office version, the date label proposal, the password reset behavior after an expired code, and the new tab announcement. He asked the developers not to close those items just because a screen reader user had found a way forward. Lena will send the observation notes to the six participants and ask them to flag any inaccurate description by Friday. The developers will receive the same notes without participant names, and the design group will get the form findings separately. The next review meeting is penciled in for May 9, but Omar said it will stay tentative until the regional office version has been checked. The audit ended with the confirmation page still open on the shared tablet and no decision about release timing.

This is the greenhouse watering rota for the second half of April and the first week of May. It covers the east house, the propagation tunnel, and the small teaching bay. The rota starts on Monday, April 15, and runs through Sunday, May 5. The printed copy is clipped beside the sink, and the working copy is in the blue folder by the time clock. Please use the working copy if a change is needed because the printed sheet is only replaced on Fridays.

On Monday and Thursday, the east house needs a full pass before the doors open at eight. The tomato beds are on the upper line, and the pepper beds are on the lower line. Please check both lines before turning the pump off. Last week, the lower line looked clear, but the end drippers on beds four and five were blocked, so check the soil with a finger as well as looking at the leaves. The young plants in the propagation tunnel need a short watering at 7:30 every morning except Sunday, when the doors stay locked and the plants are checked by the caretaker at nine.

The rota lead is Joel for this cycle, and he will collect the keys from the office on Monday. He has the cabinet key but not the padlock key for the rain tank, so the padlock key stays on the hook inside the tool cupboard. Do not leave either key in the door after watering. If Joel is away on a day, he will text the group before six, and the person listed next to his initials takes the opening check. This does not move the rest of that day's assignments.

1. Monday: Tessa waters the tomato and pepper lines and records the meter reading before and after the pump is on.
2. Tuesday: Rafael checks the propagation tunnel and waters the seed trays with the green can, not the hose, because the hose pressure lifts the labels.
3. Wednesday: Inez opens the east house and checks the pepper beds while Joel does the water meter reading.
4. Thursday: Tessa repeats the full pass and rinses the mesh filter at the tap beside the west door.
5. Friday: Rafael checks the tunnel and the teaching bay and writes any empty trays on the board beside the sink.

Saturday is the shared catch-up day, and no single person is expected to cover all three areas. Inez opens the east house, Tessa takes the tunnel, and Rafael checks the teaching bay. If someone cannot come in, they should post in the group by the evening before and ask another rota member directly rather than assuming the next person has seen the message. The person who accepts should write their initials on the working copy and tell Joel so he can check the key handover.

The water pressure gauge is beside the pump, and the normal reading is between two and three bars. If the gauge falls below 1.5 bars, stop the pump and close the blue valve before checking whether the tank is low. Last Monday, the tank was half full, but the intake screen had leaves against it, so do not refill the tank automatically and do not open the backup tap until the screen has been cleared. The backup tap draws from the teaching bay line, and using it while that line is running leaves the bay beds dry. This is important if the pressure drops during the Saturday catch-up round because the teaching bay may already have been watered, and the second pass could drain the line.

On the first Saturday of this rota, the school group arrives at ten, and their guide needs the center aisle kept dry from 9:30 onward. Water the teaching bay beds before nine and leave the watering cans on the rack by the sink, not beside the door. The group can still visit the east house if the floor is dry, but if water has pooled near the west threshold, put out the yellow floor sign and ask the guide to wait until it has drained. Nobody should carry a full tray across the wet aisle.

The rainwater tank reading should be written on the clipboard each Monday and Friday, and the date should go beside the number. Use liters, not a percentage, because the tank has a narrow bottom and the float reading is misleading when it is nearly empty. Joel said, “Last spring we kept topping it up before we knew whether the intake was blocked,” so the current plan is to inspect the screen first and report a damaged screen to facilities rather than trying to pull it out with pliers. The spare screen is in the labeled drawer under the seed bench.

If there is a leak at a hose joint, turn the small handle at that branch, not the main blue valve. Then put the orange tray under the joint and write the bed number on the maintenance card. The card is on the cupboard door. Facilities normally comes the next morning, but there is no promise of a same-day repair. While a leak is being watched, someone must stay nearby, and the pump should be switched off before leaving the house. Do not tape over a cracked hose because water can escape behind the bench and soften the wooden supports.

At the end of each shift, return the green can to the tunnel and the long-handled watering wand to the hook near the east house tap. Wipe the meter face so the next person can read it, and record any plants that look wilted even if the soil feels damp. The leaves near the north vent often curl in the afternoon because that corner gets warm, so check the stems before adding extra water. On Friday, Joel will review the working copy and send the next week's assignments before the office closes. If a name or bed number is hard to read, ask him to confirm it rather than guessing. Keep the final meter reading on the clipboard for the May 5 closeout, and leave the pump off when the last person locks the east house.
